35: - **The concealed bonus.** His sworn affidavit (2026-08-30) says bonus "discretionary; none expected," but an HR letter (2026-03-02) written five months **before** the affidavit shows a 2026 target bonus of 45,000, half paid in September, with him at 112% of plan → expected 2026 bonus **50,400** (45,000 × 1.12). Rule 16.2(e) (per `columbia_equitable_distribution.md`) requires full disclosure of income "including bonuses and expected compensation," and authorizes **sanctions including an unequal division in your favor** and reopening of a judgment procured on a false affidavit. This is your leverage, and it is not theoretical — the false statement is in a sworn filing against documents from his own employer, and the "always gets a bonus" history is exactly what the guidelines' "expected or recurring bonuses" language captures (`columbia_child_support_guidelines.md`).

For any instrument executed after December 31, 2018, that is no longer the law: alimony is neither deductible by the payor nor includible by the recipient (post-TCJA; `irc_1041_121_71.md`). Practically, that means the 72,000 comes to you **tax-free** — favorable to you; do not trade it for a "gross-up" that assumes it is taxable — but it also means he bears the full 72,000 with no offset, which is ground to push on the **36-month term**.
37: 
38: **Bottom line:** the structure (house to you, retirement account to him) can work for your goals, but only with (a) an equalization payment to you, and/or (b) the disclosure remedy. Don't sign "50/50" as drafted.

40: ## Addendum A — "It's exactly 50/50" and "you're getting the biggest asset": answering the talking points
41: 
42: You will not have to choose between protecting value and keeping the house. Nothing below requires litigation; the corrective items are negotiation asks over liquid assets, and the plan itself stays house-first.
43: 
44: 1. **"Exactly 50/50" is true in dollars and false in value — and the difference is not small.** Dollars: 770,000 = 770,000, and your lawyer-visible schedule is honest as far as it goes. Value: your half carries 156,992 of embedded selling costs + tax (66,000 + 90,992 on the eventual sale) vs his 111,040, so on value you keep 613,008 vs his 658,960 — a gap of 45,952. That gap is ≈ 6.0% of your half (45,952 ÷ 770,000), and it is robust: even at the *least favorable* sensitivity assumption for you (32% instead of 24% on his 401(k) withdrawals) he still comes out ahead by ~13,952; at 12% the gap nearly doubles to ~93,952. In living terms, 45,952 is just under one full year of the maintenance + child support he owes you (2,000 + ~2,042 ≈ 4,042 × 12 = 48,504), and roughly the size of the 2026 bonus his affidavit denies (50,400). That is the difference between a rounding item and a real one. §14-10-113(1)(d) (per `columbia_equitable_distribution.md`) makes "the tax consequences of the division to each party" part of the court's own test — the statute, not a stylistic preference, is on this side of the arithmetic.
45: 2. **"You're getting the biggest asset" is the reason the gap matters, not an answer to it.** The house's 700,000 equity is the largest single asset — which is exactly why its embedded costs (selling costs + capital gains tax on a future sale) dwarf his, and why its liquidity is weakest: after signing you would hold 50,000 cash against a 2,648/month obligation, while he holds 50,000 cash plus 300,000 of brokerage he can sell any day. "Biggest asset" is what you want for the children — it is not a premium the estate is paying you; you are in fact behind him on value under the current structure.
46: 3. **The no-war package (in priority order for your stated goal):**
47:    - *House first (never traded):* refinance with a contingency deadline in the decree; if no refinance, the co-owned deferred-sale structure (Alternative D) rather than deed-then-solo-sale. This costs him nothing in dollars and protects the thing you actually care about.
48:    - *Corrected affidavit second:* he is required to fix the sworn filing under Rule 16.2(e) regardless — framing it as getting the file right, not as aggression, and the bonus documents make any fight a bad one for him.
49:    - *Equalization third:* 23,000 of liquid cash/brokerage (3.0% of one side's share; the amount that closes the value gap, 613,008 + 23,000 ≈ his 658,960 − 23,000). This ask touches no house equity and no retirement account.
50:    - The Rule 16.2(e) *motion* (sanctions/reopening) is a card to hold, not to lead with — it is exercised only if he stonewalls the corrected affidavit.
51: 4. **Your downside is capped even if talks fail.** If no agreement is reached on the gap, the co-owned deferred sale (Plan 2/Alternative D) still leaves each side at ~619,484 with the children in place 3–6 years — so the worst realistic outcome of holding the value position is not "lose the house"; it is "make the equalization ask quietly, and keep the house either way."
52: 
53: ## 2. The house: a decision tree (built from your 2026-10 answer)
54: 
55: You want to stay 3–6 years, and you've said you don't know whether you can refinance the 400,000 mortgage on your income — and that if you can't, you'd sell. So the house plan is a tree, worked through in order:
56: 
57: **Step 1 — Resolve the refinance question *before* signing anything.** The arithmetic we can do: at an assumed 6.1% over 24 years the payment is **2,648/month** (400,000 × 0.61%/12 ÷ (1 − (1 + 0.61%/12)^−288); the rate is an assumption — your current note terms are not in the file). In **years 1–3**, against your 6,000 earnings + 2,000 maintenance + ~2,042 support ≈ 10,042/month, that is ≈ **26% of income** — and both support streams are court-ordered, which is income a lender can typically see on paper (whether and how a lender credits them is underwriting, outside this library — get **pre-approved now** and let the answer drive the tree). In **years 4–6** the cliff hits: maintenance (2,000 × 36 months) and child support (recalculated then, with the maintenance add/subtract out) both end, leaving the 2,648 payment against ≈ 6,000 of earnings — ≈ **44% of income**, before property tax, insurance, and upkeep, none of which are in the file. So even a successful refinance needs a years-4–6 plan (refinancing again, a shorter keep, or a sale at children's exit). **Lender qualification standards and pre-approval are outside the library and remain unknown** — nothing in the analysis below assumes they pass.
58: 
59: **Plan 1 — Keep via refinance (Alternative A in `division.json`; ends at ~636,008 you / ~635,960 him).** House to you; 400,000 refinanced into your name; he keeps 401(k)+brokerage and concedes **23,000** of liquid assets to equalize after-tax totals; quitclaim deed incident to the decree (no gain, §1041). Build the refinance into the decree as a **contingency**: a fixed window (e.g., 90 days) for you to close the refinance, with the fallback in Plan 2 or Plan 3 if the window lapses, and instruct that the deed passes only at/after the refinance unless you knowingly accept the joint-loan risk. The cost of this plan is deferral, not avoidance: your eventual solo sale still pays ≈91,000 tax on the 484,000 gain above your 250,000 exclusion.

You have now told us he **always** gets a bonus and that his 2025 bonus was approximately **40,000** (your recollection — no 2025 employer documents are in the file, so the amount is flagged unverified, but recurrence itself is corroborated by the letter's plan language and the stub's unexplained excess). Rule 16.2(e) (per `columbia_equitable_distribution.md`) requires full disclosure of income "including bonuses and expected compensation," and authorizes **sanctions including an unequal division in your favor** and reopening of a judgment procured on a false affidavit. This is your leverage, and it is not theoretical — the false statement is in a sworn filing against documents from his own employer, and the "always gets a bonus" history is exactly what the guidelines' "expected or recurring bonuses" language captures (`columbia_child_support_guidelines.md`).
36: - **The maintenance tax claim is wrong.** The 2,000/month × 36 months is described as "deductible to Husband and taxable to Wife." For any instrument executed after December 31, 2018, that is no longer the law: alimony is neither deductible by the payor nor includible by the recipient (post-TCJA; `irc_1041_121_71.md`). Practically, that means the 72,000 comes to you **tax-free** — favorable to you; do not trade it for a "gross-up" that assumes it is taxable — but it also means he bears the full 72,000 with no offset, which is ground to push on the **36-month term**.
37: 
38: **Bottom line:** the structure (house to you, retirement account to him) can work for your goals, but only with (a) an equalization payment to you, and/or (b) the disclosure remedy. Don't sign "50/50" as drafted.
39: 
40: ## Addendum A — "It's exactly 50/50" and "you're getting the biggest asset": answering the talking points
41: 
42: You will not have to choose between protecting value and keeping the house. Nothing below requires litigation; the corrective items are negotiation asks over liquid assets, and the plan itself stays house-first.
43: 
44: 1. **"Exactly 50/50" is true in dollars and false in value — and the difference is not small.** Dollars: 770,000 = 770,000, and your lawyer-visible schedule is honest as far as it goes. Value: your half carries 156,992 of embedded selling costs + tax (66,000 + 90,992 on the eventual sale) vs his 111,040, so on value you keep 613,008 vs his 658,960 — a gap of 45,952. That gap is ≈ 6.0% of your half (45,952 ÷ 770,000), and it is robust: even at the *least favorable* sensitivity assumption for you (32% instead of 24% on his 401(k) withdrawals) he still comes out ahead by ~13,952; at 12% the gap nearly doubles to ~93,952. In living terms, 45,952 is just under one full year of the maintenance + child support he owes you (2,000 + ~2,042 ≈ 4,042 × 12 = 48,504), and roughly the size of the 2026 bonus his affidavit denies (50,400). That is the difference between a rounding item and a real one. §14-10-113(1)(d) (per `columbia_equitable_distribution.md`) makes "the tax consequences of the division to each party" part of the court's own test — the statute, not a stylistic preference, is on this side of the arithmetic.
45: 2. **"You're getting the biggest asset" is the reason the gap matters, not an answer to it.** The house's 700,000 equity is the largest single asset — which is exactly why its embedded costs (selling costs + capital gains tax on a future sale) dwarf his, and why its liquidity is weakest: after signing you would hold 50,000 cash against a 2,648/month obligation, while he holds 50,000 cash plus 300,000 of brokerage he can sell any day. "Biggest asset" is what you want for the children — it is not a premium the estate is paying you; you are in fact behind him on value under the current structure.
46: 3. **The no-war package (in priority order for your stated goal):**
47:    - *House first (never traded):* refinance with a contingency deadline in the decree; if no refinance, the co-owned deferred-sale structure (Alternative D) rather than deed-then-solo-sale. This costs him nothing in dollars and protects the thing you actually care about.
48:    - *Corrected affidavit second:* he is required to fix the sworn filing under Rule 16.2(e) regardless — framing it as getting the file right, not as aggression, and the bonus documents make any fight a bad one for him.
49:    - *Equalization third:* 23,000 of liquid cash/brokerage (3.0% of one side's share; the amount that closes the value gap, 613,008 + 23,000 ≈ his 658,960 − 23,000). This ask touches no house equity and no retirement account.
50:    - The Rule 16.2(e) *motion* (sanctions/reopening) is a card to hold, not to lead with — it is exercised only if he stonewalls the corrected affidavit.
51: 4. **Your downside is capped even if talks fail.** If no agreement is reached on the gap, the co-owned deferred sale (Plan 2/Alternative D) still leaves each side at ~619,484 with the children in place 3–6 years — so the worst realistic outcome of holding the value position is not "lose the house"; it is "make the equalization ask quietly, and keep the house either way."
52: 
53: ## 2. The house: a decision tree (built from your 2026-10 answer)
54: 
55: You want to stay 3–6 years, and you've said you don't know whether you can refinance the 400,000 mortgage on your income — and that if you can't, you'd sell. So the house plan is a tree, worked through in order:
56: 
57: **Step 1 — Resolve the refinance question *before* signing anything.** The arithmetic we can do: at an assumed 6.1% over 24 years the payment is **2,648/month** (400,000 × 0.61%/12 ÷ (1 − (1 + 0.61%/12)^−288); the rate is an assumption — your current note terms are not in the file). In **years 1–3**, against your 6,000 earnings + 2,000 maintenance + ~2,042 support ≈ 10,042/month, that is ≈ **26% of income** — and both support streams are court-ordered, which is income a lender can typically see on paper (whether and how a lender credits them is underwriting, outside this library — get **pre-approved now** and let the answer drive the tree). In **years 4–6** the cliff hits: maintenance (2,000 × 36 months) and child support (recalculated then, with the maintenance add/subtract out) both end, leaving the 2,648 payment against ≈ 6,000 of earnings — ≈ **44% of income**, before property tax, insurance, and upkeep, none of which are in the file. So even a successful refinance needs a years-4–6 plan (refinancing again, a shorter keep, or a sale at children's exit). **Lender qualification standards and pre-approval are outside the library and remain unknown** — nothing in the analysis below assumes they pass.
58: 
59: **Plan 1 — Keep via refinance (Alternative A in `division.json`; ends at ~636,008 you / ~635,960 him).** House to you; 400,000 refinanced into your name; he keeps 401(k)+brokerage and concedes **23,000** of liquid assets to equalize after-tax totals; quitclaim deed incident to the decree (no gain, §1041). Build the refinance into the decree as a **contingency**: a fixed window (e.g., 90 days) for you to close the refinance, with the fallback in Plan 2 or Plan 3 if the window lapses, and instruct that the deed passes only at/after the refinance unless you knowingly accept the joint-loan risk. The cost of this plan is deferral, not avoidance: your eventual solo sale still pays ≈91,000 tax on the 484,000 gain above your 250,000 exclusion.
60: 
61: **Plan 2 — Stay-then-sell with BOTH of you still on title — new "Alternative D," the fallback if you can't refinance.** Failing the refinance does **not** force you into either "sell now" or "sell later alone at a much bigger tax bill." There is a third structure: after the decree, **both of you remain on title**, the decree grants you **exclusive occupancy under the divorce instrument**, and the house is sold when the children leave (3–6 years). Reading the library's text of §121(b)(1) (each individual may exclude 250,000) with §121(d)(3)(A) (an individual is treated as using the property as a principal residence during any period of *ownership* while the spouse or former spouse is granted use under a *divorce instrument*), each former co-owner who is still an owner at sale may claim his or her own 250,000 — a combined **500,000 exclusion with no joint return and no marriage**. Arithmetic at today's values: gain 734,000 → 367,000 per co-owner (decree must fix the shares; analysis assumes equal) → each (367,000 − 250,000) × 18.8% = 21,996 → **total tax 43,992**, net 590,008, **each side 619,484** — exactly what a joint pre-decree sale produces (§1041/§121 per `irc_1041_121_71.md`; the (d)(3)(A) reading is our application of the library's excerpt, nothing in the library contradicts it). That is ≈ **47,000 better** than you owning alone at sale (tax 90,992 in the base case) while keeping the children in place. Mechanics that must be drafted: expense allocation (mortgage, taxes, insurance, repairs) with a contribution ledger; an exit trigger (listing at children's exit, or either side may buy out at appraised value); and how sale proceeds divide. Trade-offs, flagged: his name stays on a 2,648/month obligation (leverage for cooperation, less control for you); future house value moves both of you together; expense-sharing terms shift real recoveries and are not priced here.
62: 
63: **Plan 3 — Sell now, before the decree, on a joint return (Alternative B; 619,484 each).** Identical numbers to Plan 2, but the children change homes immediately and you must stay married through the sale year (filing status fixed by December 31 status). It is the same economics as Plan 2 with worse fit to your goal — it belongs at the end of the tree, used only if co-ownership until exit is truly impossible.
64: 
65: **The one structure to refuse:** a decree that transfers the whole house to you, removes his name from nothing or from title with no refinance contingency, and leaves you to sell later as sole owner if things go wrong. That combination takes ~91,000 of tax instead of ~44,000, i.e., it gifts ≈47,000 to the estate's tax bill, while you carry the entire payment risk on a joint note. If a refinance is not in hand, the deed structure and the contingency *are* the deal.
66: 
67: **Watch liquidity under every plan:** the current proposal leaves you 50,000 cash against a 2,648/month obligation. Prefer cash/brokerage equalization over slicing the pre-tax 401(k): a QDRO slice rolls to an IRA and is taxed at *your* rate — unstated in the library, so its present value is unverified. Separately, put the **February 2027 bonus installment** (≈25,200) on the table: work performed during marriage (assumption flagged: consistent with the schedule treating his 401(k), which "accrued entirely during marriage," as marital; the library does not define marital-vs-separate boundaries).
68: 
69: ## 3. What instruments are needed (none of this is "just sign the deed")
70: 
71: - **QDRO** (`qdro_72t.md`): the 401(k) is a qualified plan; any division must be made by a qualified domestic relations order. Today's proposal gives you none of it, but (a) any equalization slice from the 401(k) must be by QDRO; (b) a QDRO naming you alternate payee is the standard protection until every obligation under the decree is paid. Under a QDRO, distributions to you escape the §72(t) 10% penalty (§72(t)(2)(C)) and roll over to an IRA. Distinguish: an *IRA* is divided incident to divorce without a QDRO (§408(d)(6)); the 401(k) needs the order.
72: - **Refinance + quitclaim deed + decree order of operations:** refinance first, or decree with a deadline and a pay-off/purchase-price structure at refi (a promissory note if he carries your pay-off). Removing the joint note is as important as being on the deed: on a joint mortgage you are personally liable for 2,648/month whether or not you live there.
73: - **Form 8332** (`filing_status_dependents.md`): only sign it if you *choose* to release dependency years to him — see §5. Its default absence preserves the credits for you.
74: - **Corrected financial affidavit / Rule 16.2(e) motion:** the nondisclosure remedy runs through his corrected affidavit, disclosure of the bonus plan document, and (if he stonewalls) the sanctions/reopening procedure.
75: 
76: ## 4. Child support: his number is low, and here is the correct one
77: 
78: His counsel proposes support on salary of 168,000 and your 72,000. The guidelines (`columbia_child_support_guidelines.md`) include **expected or recurring bonuses evidenced by employer documents** — the HR letter qualifies — and add/subtract maintenance between the parties.
79: 
80: **Correct worksheet (recommended):** Husband gross 218,400 (168,000 + 50,400 bonus); Wife gross 96,000 (72,000 + 24,000 maintenance). Net = gross × 0.78 ÷ 12: Husband 12,636, Wife 6,240, combined 18,876 → basic obligation 3,050 (bracket ≤ 20,000). His share: 3,050 × 12,636/18,876 = **2,042/month** — which is *less to him than* the naive salary-only figure (2,135) *because* the maintenance he pays shifts income to you, but he in fact tops up with bonus income he denies existing. Range across scenarios (see `child_support.json`): 1,830 (salary only + maintenance) to 2,294 (bonus, no maintenance credit); bonus at the 2025 level you recall (≈40,000 — client recollection, unverified) → his gross 208,000, share **2,004**. Every scenario stays in the 3,050 bracket, so the fight is over shares. Note the guidelines include expected **or recurring** bonuses, and you have confirmed the bonuses recur ("always") — so his counsel's salary-only worksheet contradicts the guideline text twice over. He is non-residential (~30% of nights, below the 35% shared-parenting threshold), so no shared-parenting adjustment.
81: 
82: **Total monthly ask on the house-keeping plan:** child support 2,042 + maintenance 2,000 = ~4,042 to you, against your 2,648 house payment on 6,000 of earnings — ≈26% of your ~10,042/month gross inflow. Workable but tight, and remember both streams and the worksheet's maintenance lines run out together at month 36: at that point the 2,648 payment stands against ≈6,000 of earnings (≈44%) — the year-4 cliff described in §2. Plan for it in the decree (e.g., step-downs, a trueing-up schedule, or Plan 2's sale-at-exit structure) rather than meeting it unprepared.
83: 
84: ## 5. Children as dependents, and your filing status
85: 
86: - Filing status is fixed by your marital status on December 31 (`filing_status_dependents.md`). If the decree enters on or before that date, you file as single or **head of household**. Head of household requires a qualifying child living with you more than half the year and that you pay more than half the cost of the home — with ~70% of nights and the house transferring to you, that is likely, though fact-dependent once the living arrangements are settled.
87: - **§152(e): you (the custodial parent) claim the children unless you release the claim on Form 8332.** His "alternating years" plan requires you to sign a release in each of his years. The release moves the **child tax credit** to him for the released years, but cannot move head-of-household status, EITC, or the dependent-care credit — those stay with you regardless. Recommended position: don't sign Form 8332 at all; if you need trade value, release only the dependency/CTC on Form 8332 for specific years, and never the credits that legally can't move anyway.
88: 
89: ## 6. What to do about the undisclosed bonus
90: 
91: 1. **Paper it now.** Demand: (a) the bonus plan document and **2025–2026** payout records — we now have your statement that 2025's bonus was ≈40,000, so the 2025 W-2/stub should either document it or contradict the affidavit anew; (b) a corrected financial affidavit; (c) tracing of the September 2026 installment (22,500–25,200, per the stub's 27,212 YTD excess) — where is it, and is it inside the 100,000 "cash" line of his schedule?
92: 2. **Add it to the estate.** The September payment received during marriage and the February 2027 installment for work performed during the marriage (assumption flagged above) should appear in the schedule before anyone signs a "50/50" chart that omits them.
93: 3. **Preserve the sanction.** Rule 16.2(e) permits an unequal division in your favor and reopening if the false affidavit surfaces later. Even if negotiations are smooth, record in the decree the corrected affidavit values and that the division was negotiated in light of the disclosure correction — this keeps the remedy alive if the "none expected" turns out to have been worse than it looks.
94: 4. **Negotiation sequence:** get the corrected affidavit *first*; then price the division (equalization ~23,000 to you); do not give disclosure concessions "in exchange" for items he was already required to produce.
95: 
96: ## 7. Where the numbers are assumed, and what's open
97: 
98: Stated assumptions (also in `division.json`): 24% marginal rate on his 401(k) withdrawals (sensitivities 12%/32% noted); 3.8% NIIT applied to taxable gains per the engagement's conservative convention; eventual house sale at today's value (future appreciation cuts both ways); 6% selling costs; maintenance accepted as proposed for worksheet purposes; 6.1% refinance rate. Per your update, you have no further information to give us, so open items are now a **flagged-unknowns registry** (see `QUESTIONS.md`): (1) **lender qualification** — you don't know whether you can refinance; underwriting standards are outside the library and unverified, so the decision tree runs on DTI arithmetic (26% years 1–3, 44% years 4–6) with pre-approval as the next real-world step; (2) **2025 bonus amount ≈40,000** — your recollection only; nothing documents it yet; (3) **decree timing** (before/after December 31, 2026) — still unknown, and it controls filing status and the availability of a joint-return sale; (4) **your marginal ordinary rate** — never stated, so a 401(k) slice's value to you is unverified; (5) **property tax, insurance, and upkeep** on the house — absent, so the affordability cliffs are understated to that degree; (6) the **Rule 16.2(e) enhanced-award quantum** — the rule's existence is in the library, its formula is not.
99: 
100: *Nothing in this memo relies on law outside `library/INDEX.md`. Where the library is silent (e.g., lender underwriting, the formula for a Rule 16.2(e) enhanced award, the book value of pre-tax dollars to you in an IRA rollover), that is stated as unverified rather than cited.*

In **years 1–3**, against your 6,000 earnings + 2,000 maintenance + ~2,042 support ≈ 10,042/month, that is ≈ **26% of income** — and both support streams are court-ordered, which is income a lender can typically see on paper (whether and how a lender credits them is underwriting, outside this library — get **pre-approved now** and let the answer drive the tree). In **years 4–6** the cliff hits: maintenance (2,000 × 36 months) and child support (recalculated then, with the maintenance add/subtract out) both end, leaving the 2,648 payment against ≈ 6,000 of earnings — ≈ **44% of income**, before property tax, insurance, and upkeep, none of which are in the file. **Plan 1 — Keep via refinance (Alternative A in `division.json`; ends at ~636,008 you / ~635,960 him).** House to you; 400,000 refinanced into your name; he keeps 401(k)+brokerage and concedes **23,000** of liquid assets to equalize after-tax totals; quitclaim deed incident to the decree (no gain, §1041). Reading the library's text of §121(b)(1) (each individual may exclude 250,000) with §121(d)(3)(A) (an individual is treated as using the property as a principal residence during any period of *ownership* while the spouse or former spouse is granted use under a *divorce instrument*), each former co-owner who is still an owner at sale may claim his or her own 250,000 — a combined **500,000 exclusion with no joint return and no marriage**. Arithmetic at today's values: gain 734,000 → 367,000 per co-owner (decree must fix the shares; analysis assumes equal) → each (367,000 − 250,000) × 18.8% = 21,996 → **total tax 43,992**, net 590,008, **each side 619,484** — exactly what a joint pre-decree sale produces (§1041/§121 per `irc_1041_121_71.md`; the (d)(3)(A) reading is our application of the library's excerpt, nothing in the library contradicts it). **Plan 3 — Sell now, before the decree, on a joint return (Alternative B; 619,484 each).** Identical numbers to Plan 2, but the children change homes immediately and you must stay married through the sale year (filing status fixed by December 31 status). It is the same economics as Plan 2 with worse fit to your goal — it belongs at the end of the tree, used only if co-ownership until exit is truly impossible.

**The one structure to refuse:** a decree that transfers the whole house to you, removes his name from nothing or from title with no refinance contingency, and leaves you to sell later as sole owner if things go wrong. That combination takes ~91,000 of tax instead of ~44,000, i.e., it gifts ≈47,000 to the estate's tax bill, while you carry the entire payment risk on a joint note. If a refinance is not in hand, the deed structure and the contingency *are* the deal.

Prefer cash/brokerage equalization over slicing the pre-tax 401(k): a QDRO slice rolls to an IRA and is taxed at *your* rate — unstated in the library, so its present value is unverified. Separately, put the **February 2027 bonus installment** (≈25,200) on the table: work performed during marriage (assumption flagged: consistent with the schedule treating his 401(k), which "accrued entirely during marriage," as marital; the library does not define marital-vs-separate boundaries).

- **QDRO** (`qdro_72t.md`): the 401(k) is a qualified plan; any division must be made by a qualified domestic relations order. ## 6. What to do about the undisclosed bonus

1. **Paper it now.** Demand: (a) the bonus plan document and **2025–2026** payout records — we now have your statement that 2025's bonus was ≈40,000, so the 2025 W-2/stub should either document it or contradict the affidavit anew; (b) a corrected financial affidavit; (c) tracing of the September 2026 installment (22,500–25,200, per the stub's 27,212 YTD excess) — where is it, and is it inside the 100,000 "cash" line of his schedule?

## 7. Where the numbers are assumed, and what's open

Stated assumptions (also in `division.json`): 24% marginal rate on his 401(k) withdrawals (sensitivities 12%/32% noted); 3.8% NIIT applied to taxable gains per the engagement's conservative convention; eventual house sale at today's value (future appreciation cuts both ways); 6% selling costs; maintenance accepted as proposed for worksheet purposes; 6.1% refinance rate. Prefer cash/brokerage equalization over slicing the pre-tax 401(k): a QDRO slice rolls to an IRA and is taxed at *your* rate — unstated in the library, so its present value is unverified. 30: 
31: **Gap: Husband is 45,952 better off after tax** (613,008 vs 658,960) — ≈ 6.0% of your half (45,952 ÷ 770,000), ≈ 3.6% of the estate's after-tax total. His side costs 111,040 in embedded tax (15.4% of what he takes); your side costs 156,992 (22.4% of the house equity: 66,000 selling costs + 90,992 tax). "50/50" in dollars is **not** 50/50 in value. Col. Rev. Stat. §14-10-113(1)(d) (per `columbia_equitable_distribution.md`) expressly requires the court to consider "the tax consequences of the division to each party," so this disparity is a direct statutory argument, not a stylistic quibble.
32: 
33: Two additional pressures on the numbers:
34: 
35: - **The concealed bonus.** His sworn affidavit (2026-08-30) says bonus "discretionary; none expected," but an HR letter (2026-03-02) written five months **before** the affidavit shows a 2026 target bonus of 45,000, half paid in September, with him at 112% of plan → expected 2026 bonus **50,400** (45,000 × 1.12). The September 15 pay stub corroborates: YTD gross 146,212 vs salary prorate 119,000 = **27,212 unexplained**, in the range of a 22,500–25,200 September installment. You have now told us he **always** gets a bonus and that his 2025 bonus was approximately **40,000** (your recollection — no 2025 employer documents are in the file, so the amount is flagged unverified, but recurrence itself is corroborated by the letter's plan language and the stub's unexplained excess). Rule 16.2(e) (per `columbia_equitable_distribution.md`) requires full disclosure of income "including bonuses and expected compensation," and authorizes **sanctions including an unequal division in your favor** and reopening of a judgment procured on a false affidavit. This is your leverage, and it is not theoretical — the false statement is in a sworn filing against documents from his own employer, and the "always gets a bonus" history is exactly what the guidelines' "expected or recurring bonuses" language captures (`columbia_child_support_guidelines.md`).
36: - **The maintenance tax claim is wrong.** The 2,000/month × 36 months is described as "deductible to Husband and taxable to Wife." For any instrument executed after December 31, 2018, that is no longer the law: alimony is neither deductible by the payor nor includible by the recipient (post-TCJA; `irc_1041_121_71.md`). Practically, that means the 72,000 comes to you **tax-free** — favorable to you; do not trade it for a "gross-up" that assumes it is taxable — but it also means he bears the full 72,000 with no offset, which is ground to push on the **36-month term**.
37: 
38: **Bottom line:** the structure (house to you, retirement account to him) can work for your goals, but only with (a) an equalization payment to you, and/or (b) the disclosure remedy. Don't sign "50/50" as drafted.
39: 
40: ## Addendum A — "It's exactly 50/50" and "you're getting the biggest asset": answering the talking points
41: 
42: You will not have to choose between protecting value and keeping the house. Nothing below requires litigation; the corrective items are negotiation asks over liquid assets, and the plan itself stays house-first.
43:
